name: Mozilla Technology Fund — AI Auditing Tools
description: The Mozilla Technology Fund (MTF) supports projects that provide tools and resources to auditors working to create greater accountability for AI systems. Winners contribute to the Open Source Audit Tooling (OAT) Initiative (led by Mozilla Fellow Deb Raji). Mozilla defines 'audit tools' broadly: benchmarks/datasets, analysis tools, crowdsourcing tools, documentation templates, and frameworks. Applications typically open in a September–October window each cycle; all outputs must be open source.

people.name: Mehan Jayasuriya
people.role: Senior Program Officer, Mozilla Technology Fund

people.name: Deborah Raji
people.role: Mozilla Fellow — Open Source Audit Tooling (OAT) lead

logistics.decisionTimeline: Two-stage (LOI → invited full application via Fluxx). Mozilla typically communicates decisions within ~1–2 months of the deadline — e.g. an early-October close tends to yield November notifications and contracting.
logistics.grantPeriod: 12-month cohort — monthly virtual convenings plus at least one in-person gathering (MozFest).
constraints: All code must be released open source; content under Creative Commons
Award up to $50,000 (annual pool $300K–$500K)
Deliverable must be an AI audit tool aligned with the Open Source Audit Tooling (OAT) Initiative
Applicants generally need a working prototype and a team ready to execute over 12 months
Cohort participation required (monthly calls + MozFest convening)

fundedExamples.project: Mozilla-led community (Deb Raji, Abeba Birhane, Briana Vecchione, Ryan Steed, Victor Ojewale) building shared standards and tooling for auditing AI systems.
fundedExamples.takeaway: The community your MTF deliverable must plug into — align any ETC audit tool with OAT standards.

fundedExamples.project: Open-source auditing tools, e.g. a crowdsourcing tool to externally inspect a platform's pricing/recommendation model, and an 'observatory' letting journalists see what content is promoted or suppressed.
fundedExamples.takeaway: Model an ETC proposal on one concrete, reusable audit tool — not a broad platform.

fundedExamples.project: Bias/transparency projects across South Africa, Japan, and the Netherlands — crowdsourcing tools measuring unfair voice-assistant outcomes and exposing social-media recommendation engines.
fundedExamples.takeaway: Shows the scope MTF funds at $50K — a focused, shippable tool with a clear accountability use.

criteria.label: Mission alignment
criteria.rationale: AI auditing/transparency touches ETC's AI-safety and trust-infrastructure interests, but algorithmic-accountability audit tooling is not one of ETC's current projects or core humanitarian focus areas (migration, forced labor, disaster, cultural heritage). Alignment is tangential unless ETC deliberately frames an audit tool for a human-rights use case.

criteria.label: Funding fit
criteria.rationale: $50K is modest but usable for prototyping and researcher time, and Mozilla's broad definition of 'audit tools' (datasets, frameworks, analysis tools) fits ETC's applied-build model. The open-source output requirement is compatible but constrains commercialization/partner deployment.

criteria.label: Competitiveness
criteria.rationale: The MTF/OAT applicant pool is dominated by specialized AI-accountability and open-source audit-tooling teams; ETC is not primarily an AI-auditing shop and would compete against purpose-built projects. NYU/Microsoft backing helps credibility but does not offset the topical mismatch.

criteria.label: Effort / feasibility
criteria.rationale: Mozilla Technology Fund applications are relatively lightweight compared to federal or large foundation grants, and reporting is manageable, so the bandwidth cost is moderate.

criteria.label: Strategic value
criteria.rationale: Winning would connect ETC to Mozilla's accountability network and Deb Raji's OAT initiative, building AI-transparency credibility—valuable but adjacent to ETC's core human-rights intervention portfolio and unlikely to directly extend current projects.

redFlags: Core topic (AI auditing tools for algorithmic accountability) sits outside ETC's humanitarian intervention wheelhouse—fit requires reframing a project around a human-rights audit use case.
Mandatory open-source output may conflict with partner/agency deployment models ETC often uses.
Small award ($50K) relative to the strategic effort of entering a competitive, specialized applicant field.
Only worth pursuing if ETC has a concrete audit-tool concept tied to migration, forced labor, or traceability ready to propose.
scoring.summary: This Mozilla fund targets open-source AI-auditing tools for algorithmic accountability—adjacent to ETC's AI-safety and trust-infrastructure interests but off its humanitarian intervention core, and against a specialized applicant pool ETC would not naturally lead. The $50K and light application make it low-cost to attempt, but only pursue if ETC can credibly frame an audit tool for a human-rights use case (e.g., supply-chain traceability or forced-labor detection); otherwise pass and reserve bandwidth for higher-alignment opportunities.

recommendations.strategy: This is a reach grant: Mozilla's MTF funds narrowly-scoped, open-source AI audit tools that plug into Deb Raji's OAT Initiative, and ETC's humanitarian intervention model only fits if you reframe an existing project as a concrete auditing tool for a human-rights use case. Your one credible entry point is the Traceability project (verifiable ethical claims in supply chains) recast as an open-source tool that lets auditors detect forced-labor or greenwashing in algorithmic/supply-chain claims — do NOT propose a broad platform. Only pursue if you can commit to a working prototype, a 12-month cohort obligation (monthly calls + MozFest), and fully open-source/CC release; if partner deployment models require closed code, walk away now rather than burn writing bandwidth on a $50K long shot.

tips.title: Reframe Traceability as an auditor-facing tool, not a supply-chain platform
tips.detail: MTF funds tools FOR auditors creating accountability, not intervention systems. Recast your supply-chain traceability work as a benchmark/dataset or analysis tool that lets labor-rights auditors verify or falsify a company's ethical-sourcing claims — a concrete, reusable audit artifact in the spirit of the 2023 'observatory' and pricing-inspection tools.

tips.title: Resolve the open-source conflict before you write a word
tips.detail: Every line of code must ship open source and content under Creative Commons — this collides with the closed partner/agency deployment models ETC often uses. Confirm with your intended partner (and Microsoft Research collaborators) that the specific audit tool can be fully OSS, or the proposal is dead on arrival.

tips.title: Anchor explicitly to the OAT Initiative and its people
tips.detail: Winners must contribute to the Open Source Audit Tooling Initiative led by Deb Raji (with Birhane, Vecchione, Steed, Ojewale). Read OAT's published standards and name how your tool plugs into them — reviewers reward interoperability with the existing community, not a standalone artifact.

tips.title: Match the $50K scope: one shippable tool, not a research agenda
tips.detail: The 2022–2023 cohorts funded tightly-scoped, shippable tools (crowdsourced voice-assistant bias measurement, a content-promotion observatory). Scope your deliverable to something a small team can build and release in 12 months, and lead with the specific accountability decision it enables for a named auditor type.

tips.title: Use the pre-deadline window to test fit with Mozilla/OAT
tips.detail: Applications open ~Sept 6 for an Oct 5 close. Before then, engage the OAT community (public channels, MozFest presence, Deb Raji's published work) to sanity-check whether a forced-labor/traceability audit tool is welcome — this de-risks a low-probability bet and signals you're a genuine community contributor.

tips.title: Lead with a working prototype, not a concept
tips.detail: MTF applicants 'generally need a working prototype.' Show a demonstrable slice of your traceability tooling now and evidence your interdisciplinary team (policy + technical prototyping, CGA + Microsoft Research) can execute over 12 months — this is where ETC's applied-prototyping strength is your real differentiator over pure-tech applicants.

tips.title: Plan for the two-stage Fluxx flow and cohort commitment
tips.detail: This is LOI → invited full application via Fluxx, with monthly virtual convenings and mandatory MozFest attendance. Confirm a named team member can carry the cohort obligations for a full year before committing, and map backward from the Oct 5 LOI so the invited full app isn't rushed.

tips.title: Frame the $50K around researcher/build time, honestly
tips.detail: The award is small and NYU overhead could swallow it — structure the budget toward developer/researcher time to build and release the open tool, and confirm ETC's constraint of funding staff time over pure overhead can be honored within Mozilla's allowable costs.

tips.title: Be willing to defer if no concrete tool concept is ready
tips.detail: With fit at 49/100 and win probability ~15%, this is only worth it if a specific migration/forced-labor/traceability audit-tool concept is already crystallized. If it isn't by early September, skip this cycle — MTF runs annually, so a stronger prototype next year beats a thin one now.

actionItems: Convene the Traceability team to decide if a single, OSS-releasable auditor-facing tool (e.g. a forced-labor claims-verification benchmark or analysis tool) can be defined and prototyped — go/no-go on pursuing this cycle.
Get written confirmation from the relevant partner/agency and Microsoft Research that the specific tool can be fully open source under CC before drafting.
Read the OAT Initiative's published standards and 2022–2023 MTF winners in detail, and draft one paragraph on how ETC's tool interoperates with OAT.
Engage the OAT/Mozilla community informally (or via MozFest channels) to test-fit the forced-labor/traceability audit concept before the September opening.
Assemble prototype evidence and name the team member who will own the 12-month cohort commitment, then map an internal timeline backward from the Oct 5 LOI.
Draft a tight, single-tool LOI scoped to the $50K/12-month envelope, with a budget weighted toward build/research time.

name: Humanity AI — Public Open Call
description: Humanity AI is a $500M, five-year pooled philanthropic fund (Ford, MacArthur, Omidyar, Mellon, Mozilla, Doris Duke, Lumina, Kapor, Packard, and Siegel) ensuring AI is shaped by and for people. After $18M in inaugural 2026 grants ($500K each to orgs like AI Now, Data & Society, New America), the coalition is launching a ~$10M public open call in summer 2026 prioritizing communities closest to AI's impact. Focus spans democracy, security, labor/economy, education, and arts & culture. Fiscal sponsor: Rockefeller Philanthropy Advisors.

people.name: John Palfrey
people.role: Co-chair, Humanity AI; President, MacArthur Foundation

people.name: Michele Lawrence Jawando
people.role: Co-chair, Humanity AI; President, Omidyar Network

logistics.decisionTimeline: Open-call review timeline not yet announced (the ~$10M public call launches summer 2026). The inaugural round moved from announcement to award over several months.
logistics.grantPeriod: Part of a 5-year, $500M initiative; individual grant terms TBD (inaugural grants were $500K each).
constraints: ~$10M reserved across this open call's grantees
Prioritizes organizations and communities closest to AI's impact (US focus)
Fiscal sponsor: Rockefeller Philanthropy Advisors
Highly competitive — inaugural cohort was large, established national institutions

fundedExamples.project: Advancing AI transparency and accountability
fundedExamples.takeaway: Example of a policy/accountability organization funded to advance AI transparency and public interest.

criteria.label: Mission alignment
criteria.rationale: Humanity AI's focus on labor/economy, arts & culture, security, and public-interest AI maps well onto ETC's forced-labor, cultural-heritage, migration, and traceability work; the human-centered 'AI by and for people' framing is squarely in ETC's wheelhouse.

criteria.label: Funding fit
criteria.rationale: $500K philanthropic awards to organizations doing applied, community-facing AI work fit ETC's need to fund researcher/staff time and prototyping; foundation pooled funds typically allow program and personnel costs rather than just overhead.

criteria.label: Competitiveness
criteria.rationale: Inaugural grants went to established policy/advocacy institutions (AI Now, Data & Society, New America) and the open call explicitly prioritizes 'communities closest to AI's impact,' which may favor community-led over academic labs; ~20 awards against a very large national applicant pool makes this highly competitive despite ETC's strong NYU CGA backing.

criteria.label: Effort / feasibility
criteria.rationale: A public open call is generally lighter than a full RFP, but a coalition of ten major foundations will demand a polished, community-impact-forward proposal and rigorous reporting; deadline is only loosely defined (summer 2026), giving lead time.

criteria.label: Strategic value
criteria.rationale: Winning would connect ETC to a ten-foundation coalition (Ford, MacArthur, Omidyar, Mozilla, Packard, etc.), diversifying beyond Microsoft Research and building deep philanthropic relationships that compound across future public-interest AI work.

redFlags: Coalition emphasis on 'community power' and 'communities closest to AI's impact' may disadvantage a university/corporate-backed research lab versus community-led applicants
ETC's Microsoft Research affiliation could create optics friction with a philanthropic fund positioning AI as shaped by-and-for people against Big Tech influence
Inaugural awardees were established policy/advocacy institutions, signaling a possible preference away from applied-prototyping labs
Only ~20 awards nationally against a broad open-call pool makes odds long despite good thematic fit
scoring.summary: Strong thematic fit (labor rights, cultural heritage, public-interest AI) and exceptional strategic upside from tapping a ten-foundation coalition make this worth pursuing, with a $500K award that suits ETC's applied-research-plus-prototyping model. The main risks are competitiveness—inaugural grants favored established advocacy orgs and the call prioritizes community-led groups—and possible optics tension with ETC's Microsoft ties. Recommend applying with a proposal that foregrounds affected-community partnership and centers a specific project (e.g., forced-labor traceability or cultural-heritage return) rather than institutional capacity.

availabilityNote: Public open call ($10M) launches Summer 2026 — watch for dates

coalition.name: John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation

submission.mechanism: No open application portal yet; organizations sign up for updates to receive details on how to apply. Grants managed via pooled fund by Rockefeller Philanthropy Advisors.
steps: Sign up for updates on the Humanity AI website
Await announcement of open call / application details
submission.notes: A $10 million open call was announced as forthcoming alongside the inaugural grants.

name: AI & Data for Social Good Grants
description: PJMF is a global philanthropy advancing AI and data science for a thriving, equitable, sustainable future. 2026 grants (typically $200K–$750K) span 'Data as a Public Good', Journalism & Media, Solidarity, Climate, and Health — e.g., $250K to Public Health Watch for AI-assisted pollution accountability. PJMF largely identifies grantees proactively rather than through an open application portal.

logistics.decisionTimeline: No fixed cycle — PJMF reviews on a rolling basis and largely sources grantees itself; expect a multi-month cultivation before a decision.
constraints: No open application portal — access is primarily by invitation / relationship
Nonprofit organizations globally
Priorities: Data as a Public Good, Journalism & Media, Solidarity, Climate, Health

fundedExamples.project: Community tools to collect and share local pollution + health data and explore AI to hold polluters accountable, feeding investigative journalism.
fundedExamples.takeaway: Nearly ETC's model — AI for accountability plus community data. A strong template to adapt.

fundedExamples.project: Expand expert-led AI journalism and public AI literacy at scale.
fundedExamples.takeaway: Shows PJMF funds AI-literacy / public-education work ETC could propose.

fundedExamples.project: Open-source modeling infrastructure for auditable carbon-removal accountability.
fundedExamples.takeaway: 'Auditable accountability infrastructure' framing maps directly onto ETC's strengths.

criteria.label: Mission alignment
criteria.rationale: PJMF's 'Data as a Public Good', Climate, Solidarity, and digital-equity portfolios map closely onto ETC's humanitarian tech, climate accountability, traceability, and trust-infrastructure work. AI-for-social-good framing fits ETC's applied intervention model directly.

criteria.label: Funding fit
criteria.rationale: The $200K–$750K range and social-good focus support applied research, prototyping, and staff time — exactly ETC's needs. The $250K pollution-accountability example shows PJMF funds precisely this kind of intervention work.

criteria.label: Competitiveness
criteria.rationale: ETC's NYU CGA + Microsoft Research backing is credible, but PJMF largely selects grantees proactively rather than via open competition, so the main hurdle is getting on their radar rather than out-writing rivals.

criteria.label: Effort / feasibility
criteria.rationale: No open application portal means effort shifts from proposal-writing to relationship cultivation and warm introductions, which is uncertain and hard to time; reporting burden itself would be moderate.

criteria.label: Strategic value
criteria.rationale: PJMF is a prestigious, well-networked global philanthropy; a relationship would compound across ETC's climate, traceability, and migration projects and open doors to future funding and partners.

redFlags: PJMF largely identifies grantees proactively and lacks an open application portal, so a cold application is unlikely to succeed without a warm introduction
No stated deadline or intake process makes timing and pipeline planning difficult
scoring.summary: Strong mission and funding fit — PJMF's data-and-AI-for-social-good portfolio aligns well with ETC's humanitarian and climate-accountability work, and the award size suits applied prototyping. The key obstacle is that PJMF funds mostly by proactive selection, so ETC should invest in relationship-building and warm introductions (leveraging NYU CGA and Microsoft Research networks) rather than a speculative cold application.

availabilityNote: No open portal; relationship-based, occasional themed RFPs

name: Technology & Society Grants
description: Ford's Technology and Society program backs equal access to and fair regulation of digital technology — advancing transparency, privacy, access to knowledge, and free expression, and protecting civil and human rights online. Ford also anchors the Public Interest Technology (PIT) field and co-founds Humanity AI. Ford funds by invitation/relationship rather than open calls, and is mid-leadership transition (Heather Gerken succeeds Darren Walker as President).

logistics.decisionTimeline: No open cycle — funding follows relationship-building and can take months to over a year.

keyDates.label: Leadership transition — Heather Gerken becomes President

constraints: No open application portal — Ford funds by invitation / relationship
Institution-scale grants; highly competitive
Mid-leadership transition may shift Technology & Society priorities

fundedExamples.project: Research + advocacy on how tech worsens racial/economic inequality; built the Benefits Tech Advocacy Hub, exposing automated systems that denied home-care benefits to up to 66% of eligible people.
fundedExamples.takeaway: The clearest ETC analog at Ford — algorithmic accountability in public benefits. Study their research+advocacy model.

fundedExamples.project: Open-source anonymous whistleblowing platform for journalists and sources.
fundedExamples.takeaway: Example of the durable open-source public-interest tooling Ford's PIT work backs.

fundedExamples.project: Independent research institute on technology's social implications (Ford was a founding funder).
fundedExamples.takeaway: Shows Ford funds applied tech-and-society research institutions.

criteria.label: Mission alignment
criteria.rationale: Ford's public-interest-tech and digital-rights framing overlaps ETC's civic tech, trust infrastructure, and information equity work, and its human-rights-online focus is adjacent — but its core priorities (privacy, free expression, digital rights) don't directly fund ETC's flagship migration, forced-labor, disaster-response, or cultural-heritage projects.

criteria.label: Funding fit
criteria.rationale: $250k is a solid, right-sized award for applied research and prototyping, and Ford routinely funds project and general support that covers researcher/staff time rather than pure overhead.

criteria.label: Competitiveness
criteria.rationale: Ford funds by invitation and existing relationship, not open calls; without an established Ford tie ETC cannot simply apply, and the mid-leadership transition adds uncertainty despite strong NYU CGA + Microsoft backing.

criteria.label: Effort / feasibility
criteria.rationale: The real cost is relationship-building and securing an invitation rather than a proposal per se — a slow, high-touch process that strains limited bandwidth with no guaranteed entry point.

criteria.label: Strategic value
criteria.rationale: Ford anchors the PIT field and co-founds Humanity AI; a relationship or grant would be highly prestigious and open compounding doors across the public-interest-tech ecosystem.

redFlags: Ford funds by invitation/relationship, not open calls — ETC has no stated existing Ford relationship, so there is no direct application pathway.
Mid-leadership transition (Gerken succeeding Walker) creates strategic uncertainty about near-term priorities.
Program's stated priorities (privacy, free expression, digital rights) are adjacent but do not squarely fund ETC's core migration/forced-labor/disaster/cultural-heritage projects.
scoring.summary: Ford is a prestigious, well-sized funder whose public-interest-tech mission is genuinely adjacent to ETC's civic-tech and human-rights work, but it funds only by invitation and is mid-leadership transition, so there is no open door to apply. Treat this as a long-term relationship-cultivation target — pursue warm introductions through NYU CGA and PIT networks and frame ETC's trust-infrastructure/information-equity angle — rather than a near-term proposal. Do not spend scarce grant-writing bandwidth on a formal application until an invitation pathway exists.

availabilityNote: Ford does not accept unsolicited proposals

logistics.decisionTimeline: 3–12 month relationship-building process before any decision; SFE reaches out rather than accepting applications.
constraints: Does NOT accept unsolicited proposals — SFE staff author the proposal after a relationship forms
Focus lanes: Learning, Workforce, Infrastructure
Values networked introductions from existing grantees

fundedExamples.project: Building digital-economy capacity and tech ecosystems in rural communities.
fundedExamples.takeaway: Siegel's community-tech / infrastructure lane — frame ETC work around infrastructure + equity.

fundedExamples.project: Expanding access to computing and tech careers for women and underrepresented students.
fundedExamples.takeaway: A computing-equity example at ETC's scale (~$250K) — a realistic size to target.

fundedExamples.grantee: MIT — Siegel Family Quest for Intelligence
fundedExamples.project: Academic research on intelligence and its societal impact.
fundedExamples.takeaway: Signals Siegel's research bent — pair any ETC ask with a knowledge-building output.

criteria.label: Mission alignment

The strongest bridges are labor rights under Workforce and trust/digital infrastructure under Infrastructure.

criteria.label: Funding fit
criteria.rationale: $250K is a healthy award size and SFE's inquiry-driven model supports applied research and staff time rather than pure overhead, which fits ETC's needs well.

criteria.label: Competitiveness
criteria.rationale: SFE does not accept unsolicited proposals and funds only after a 3–12 month relationship; ETC has no established tie to SFE, so realistic near-term competitiveness is low despite strong NYU/Microsoft backing.

redFlags: No unsolicited proposals — funding requires a pre-existing 3–12 month relationship ETC does not appear to have
Funder pillars (Learning, Workforce, Infrastructure) only partially overlap ETC's humanitarian/human-rights focus
No deadline or clear entry point means an uncertain, relationship-dependent timeline rather than a discrete application
scoring.summary: Siegel is a prestigious, well-resourced tech-and-society funder whose $250K inquiry-driven grants fit ETC's applied-research model, but the mission overlap is partial and, critically, SFE only funds after a months-long cultivated relationship it does not currently have with ETC. Treat this as a long-game relationship-building target—identify a warm introduction and frame ETC's labor-rights/trust-infrastructure work against SFE's Workforce/Infrastructure pillars—rather than a near-term application worth heavy proposal effort.

availabilityNote: Siegel is inquiry/invite-based; no open portal

name: AWS Imagine Grant for Nonprofits
description: An annual open call funding US 501(c) nonprofits that use technology in new or expanded ways (pilots, proofs of concept, or scaling existing programs). Three tiers: Pathfinder (up to $200K unrestricted + $100K AWS credits), Go Further Faster (up to $150K + $100K credits), Momentum to Modernize (up to $50K + $20K credits). Welcomes all mission areas and is technology-agnostic (not AI-only). 2026 Round One closed 5 June 2026 — recurring annually (portal typically opens ~March).

logistics.decisionTimeline: Two-round process. 2026 portal opened 19 March, Round One closed 5 June; Round One status notified by 14 July 2026. Expect ~1 month from close to advancement notice.
logistics.grantPeriod: Project-based; unrestricted cash plus AWS credits and technical support.
constraints: US 501(c) nonprofits only; educational institutions excluded
Half the package is AWS promotional credits, not cash
Project must use technology in a new or expanded way

criteria.label: Mission alignment
criteria.rationale: The grant is technology-agnostic and welcomes all mission areas including civic tech and innovation, which comfortably covers ETC's applied-tech-for-good work, but it is not specifically oriented toward humanitarian/human-rights domains, so the overlap is general rather than targeted.

criteria.label: Funding fit
criteria.rationale: Up to $200K unrestricted plus cloud credits explicitly funds pilots, proofs of concept, and scaling — an excellent match for ETC's prototyping-plus-staff-time model, with unrestricted dollars that avoid the overhead-only trap ETC wants to steer clear of.

criteria.label: Competitiveness
criteria.rationale: NYU's 501(c)(3) status and ETC's strong applied track record make it a credible applicant, but the open call draws a large, diverse nonprofit pool and ETC's deep Microsoft Research ties create a natural fit-and-optics tension with an AWS-funded, credit-based program.

criteria.label: Effort / feasibility
criteria.rationale: An annual open call is moderate lift, but a competitive Pathfinder application requires a well-scoped AWS-native project plan and the current round already closed (June 2026), meaning ETC must wait for the ~March portal reopening.

criteria.label: Strategic value
criteria.rationale: Winning would diversify ETC's cloud/funder relationships and lend a second major-tech backer, but building on AWS credits partly duplicates and could complicate its existing Microsoft Research infrastructure and partnership.

redFlags: Potential conflict/optics with ETC's existing Microsoft Research partnership — the award is AWS-funded and tied to AWS cloud credits, which pushes toward an AWS-native tech stack that may not align with ETC's current infrastructure
Current 2026 round already closed (5 June 2026); ETC would have to wait for the next annual cycle (~March), so this is not actionable immediately
Eligibility is framed around 501(c) nonprofits and their programs; a university research CoLab must apply through NYU and may be a less typical fit than a service-delivery nonprofit
Mission fit is broad/generic rather than aligned to ETC's core humanitarian focus areas, so the proposal must actively frame a specific intervention (evacuation, traceability, etc.) to stand out
scoring.summary: The AWS Imagine Grant offers attractive unrestricted funding for exactly the kind of pilots and proofs of concept ETC builds, and NYU's nonprofit status makes ETC eligible. The main caveats are moderate competitiveness in a broad open call, the tension between an AWS credit-based award and ETC's Microsoft Research infrastructure, and the fact that the current round has closed. Worth considering for the next annual cycle if ETC can frame a specific, AWS-deliverable humanitarian intervention — but not a slam-dunk priority.

name: Impact Challenge: AI for Government Innovation

logistics.decisionTimeline: Open call reviewed by Google.org, Google experts, and external partners (Renaissance Philanthropy, Centre for Public Impact); selected orgs join a multi-month accelerator. The 2026 cycle closed 3 April.
logistics.grantPeriod: Grant plus a multi-month Google.org Accelerator.
constraints: Requires partnering with a government entity
Must have a clear, explicit social-impact purpose
Individuals without an organizational affiliation are ineligible

fundedExamples.project: PROMPTS, an SMS digital-health service using AI triage for 3.8M mothers across Kenya/Sub-Saharan Africa, supporting Ministries of Health with data-driven policy decisions.

fundedExamples.project: AI decision-support tool using state/federal resilience data to help governments prioritize wildfire mitigation; shaped 300+ California wildfire resilience plans.
fundedExamples.takeaway: A government decision-support tool — the kind of accountable, policy-facing tool ETC could build.

fundedExamples.project: MobileAid: AI mobile-metadata analysis with the Government of Togo to target aid to ultra-vulnerable households during crises.

criteria.label: Mission alignment
criteria.rationale: The govtech/public-services framing overlaps ETC's agency-partnered work (evacuation/disaster response, cultural heritage return, diplomacy rehearsal), but the challenge is broadly about transforming public services rather than ETC's core humanitarian/human-rights focus — fit is real but requires shaping a project around government partnership.

criteria.label: Funding fit
criteria.rationale: $300k plus Cloud credits, pro bono technical expertise and training directly supports applied prototyping and researcher time — a strong match for ETC's build-and-test model, though academic overhead treatment under Google.org terms is unclear.

criteria.label: Competitiveness
criteria.rationale: NYU CGA credibility and applied track record help, but this is a prestigious, globally competitive challenge favoring applicants with a concrete, in-hand government partner deploying generative/agentic AI at scale — ETC would need a ready public-sector partner to be a front-runner.

criteria.label: Effort / feasibility
criteria.rationale: Impact Challenge applications are moderately heavy and the mandatory accelerator plus government-partnership requirement adds real coordination burden, though the funded prototyping work is squarely within ETC's wheelhouse.

criteria.label: Strategic value
criteria.rationale: A Google.org win adds a marquee funder, cloud/technical capabilities, and deeper government relationships that compound across the evacuation and diplomacy projects — tempered by the awkwardness of leaning on Google infrastructure while partnered with Microsoft Research.

redFlags: Requires a demonstrable government/public-sector partner deploying generative or agentic AI — ETC must have a concrete agency partner lined up to be competitive
Potential tension leveraging Google Cloud/accelerator resources given ETC's existing Microsoft Research collaboration
Emphasis on 'transforming public services' skews more general govtech than ETC's humanitarian/human-rights core, risking a diluted or off-mission proposal

proposal.title: Digital Safety Capacity for High-Risk Public-Interest Organizations
proposal.thesis: ETC proposes a two-year program delivering practical digital-safety training, threat-model assessments, and community-centered secure-tooling guidance for high-risk civil-society actors — NGOs, journalists, human-rights defenders, and anti-trafficking organizations. This aligns with the Common Good Cyber Fund's 'training' and 'protecting high-risk actors' priorities, drawing on ETC's proven strengths in capacity building for nonprofits, community and stakeholder engagement, and bridging technologists with mission-driven communities. Rather than building DNS/routing or incident-response infrastructure (which ETC does not do), we focus squarely on the human and organizational layer of public-interest cybersecurity, where our applied-research and prototyping methods add durable value. The two-year operating structure lets us stand up a repeatable, open-methodology digital-safety capacity program serving actors who are routinely targeted but under-resourced.

keyAspects.aspect: Training and capacity building for high-risk actors
keyAspects.why: The fund explicitly lists 'training' as a fundable activity and prioritizes protecting NGOs, journalists, and human-rights defenders — this is the one funded category where ETC has genuine, demonstrable capability (capacity building for nonprofits and public-interest technologists).

keyAspects.aspect: Serving high-risk digital actors via anti-trafficking work
keyAspects.why: ETC's technology-to-combat-human-trafficking focus area involves organizations and populations that are high-risk digital actors, giving a concrete, non-invented population and a credible 'direct services' angle the eligibility rules require.

Differentiates ETC from purely technical cybersecurity providers; the funder's 'technology for good' and human-rights framing rewards approaches grounded in the needs of the people being protected, not just infrastructure.

Aligns with the Internet Society Foundation's ethos of shared public-interest infrastructure and the fund's 'common good' framing — ETC can commit to openly licensed training materials and threat-model templates that scale beyond the grant.

sections.heading: Organizational overview and eligibility
sections.guidance: Confirm 501(c)(3) status and a bank account able to receive US foundation funds. Clearly frame ETC as a public-interest technology organization and state upfront which funded activity (training / protecting high-risk actors) you are delivering — do not overclaim infrastructure work.

sections.heading: Statement of need
sections.guidance: Document the digital-safety gap facing under-resourced NGOs, journalists, HRDs, and anti-trafficking organizations. Cite the mismatch between sophisticated threats these actors face and their limited security capacity — the layer ETC addresses.

sections.heading: Program design and activities
sections.guidance: Detail a concrete two-year workplan: threat-model assessments, tailored digital-safety training curricula, secure-tooling selection guidance, and open publication of methods. Be explicit that ETC delivers the human/organizational layer, partnering out or referring for infrastructure-level services (DNS/routing, incident response).

sections.heading: Target beneficiaries and reach
sections.guidance: Name the high-risk actor communities you will serve and how you will recruit them through existing ETC relationships in the anti-trafficking, arts, and nonprofit sectors. Give realistic numbers for a small senior team.

sections.heading: Team and organizational capacity
sections.guidance: Present the senior team honestly, emphasizing applied research, community engagement, and capacity-building track record. Address the bandwidth constraint by scoping deliverables tightly.

sections.heading: Budget and use of operating funds
sections.guidance: Allocate the two-year budget primarily to staff time for training delivery, assessments, and materials development — matching ETC's preference for funding applied work over overhead. Justify against the $100K–$300K range.

sections.heading: Sustainability and common-good contribution
sections.guidance: Explain how open-licensed curricula and templates create lasting public value beyond the grant, and how capacity-building support from the fund would help institutionalize the program.

alignmentHighlights: Directly addresses the fund's named 'training' activity and its mandate to protect high-risk actors (NGOs, journalists, HRDs).
ETC's anti-trafficking focus area supplies a real high-risk-actor population, satisfying the 'direct services for high-risk digital actors' eligibility requirement.
Open-source, published-output orientation matches the Internet Society Foundation's public-interest, common-good philosophy.

Human-centered, community-engaged approach complements — rather than duplicates — the infrastructure providers the fund also supports, strengthening the overall public-interest cybersecurity ecosystem.
differentiators: Bridges technologists, communities, and policymakers — few pure cybersecurity providers bring this cross-sector, human-centered lens.
Applied-research rigor with published, reusable outputs rather than one-off service delivery.
Existing trust relationships with vulnerable and high-risk communities (e.g., anti-trafficking) that infrastructure vendors typically lack.
Ethics-first framing that resonates with the fund's human-rights and 'technology for good' priorities.
risks: Core capability gap: ETC does not provide cybersecurity infrastructure (DNS/routing, threat intel, incident response); the proposal must credibly narrow to training/capacity building or the application risks being scored out of scope.

This is a two-year OPERATING grant that 'expects an established program' — ETC has not run a standing digital-safety program, so reviewers may see this as a new initiative rather than an established one; consider whether prior related work can be reframed as an existing program or whether a partner lead is wiser.

Eligibility hinges on providing 'cybersecurity infrastructure and/or direct services for high-risk digital actors' — ETC must demonstrate concrete direct-service delivery, not just research, or risk being deemed ineligible.

Tight deadline (4 August 2026) against ETC's limited grant-writing bandwidth — assess whether the ~15% win probability justifies the effort, or whether partnering with an established cyber provider (e.g., via Global Cyber Alliance network) as a training subcontractor is a higher-ROI path.
Thin direct evidence: ETC should confirm it has demonstrable digital-safety training deliverables or case examples before committing; if none exist, this is a weak fit for an operating grant.

name: Displaced Livelihoods Initiative (DLI) Grants 2026
funder: Innovations for Poverty Action (IPA) & J-PAL — Displaced Livelihoods Initiative (funded by the IKEA Foundation)
description: Round V (2026) call for proposals from the Displaced Livelihoods Initiative (DLI), managed by Innovations for Poverty Action (IPA) and the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL) and funded by the IKEA Foundation. DLI funds rigorous impact evaluations and related research on sustainable livelihoods for displacement-affected populations — refugees, asylum-seekers, stateless people, IDPs, and the communities hosting them. Grant types & maximum awards: Exploratory $10K; Pilot $75K; Full study $250K; Infrastructure & public goods $250K; Evidence Use (refugee-led orgs / researchers with lived experience) $20K; Conference Travel $4K. Off-cycle proposals up to $75K with time-sensitive justification. Priority research areas: resilience, wage employment, entrepreneurship, social cohesion & norms, rights & regulations, and measurement/design — explicitly including how data science, machine learning, satellite imagery, and AI can improve impact measurement (a natural entry point for ETC).
availabilityNote: Round V main track is closed to new applicants — the mandatory Expression of Interest was due May 15, 2026 (now passed). Full proposals (for those who filed an EOI) are due Jul 24, 2026. Off-cycle proposals up to $75K remain possible with time-sensitive justification via displacement@poverty-action.org.

logistics.decisionTimeline: Proposals reviewed after each round by a rotating group of academic (and sometimes policy) reviewers; DLI does not publish a fixed decision date.
logistics.grantPeriod: Varies by project type (exploratory through multi-year full studies).
constraints: Research team must include at least one member whose primary affiliation is a university (NYU qualifies).
Mandatory Expression of Interest was required (due May 15, 2026) before a full proposal.
All local/national/international ethics (IRB) approvals required before fieldwork; extra ethical care given the target population's vulnerability.
Funded impact evaluations must collect cost data for cost-effectiveness analysis and make per-unit program costs public.
Target group: displacement-affected populations (refugees, asylum-seekers, stateless, IDPs, and host communities).

reviewCriteria.detail: Significant contribution to knowledge; probes mechanisms (how an intervention has impact); new questions, methods, measures, or interventions; bridges practical experiment and economic theory.
Addresses DLI's priority research areas; real demand from policymakers/practitioners; generalizable 'lessons learned'; considers cost and whether the intervention scales.
Research design appropriately answers the questions; identifies and addresses threats to validity; full-study designs are powered to detect results.

Strong, durable implementing-partner relationship and track record; logistical/political/ethics feasibility; pilots show a path to a full evaluation; infrastructure projects show how they enable future research.
Study cost is commensurate with expected scientific and policy contribution; leverages funding from other sources.
Risk of harm to participants/staff and mitigation strategy; all approvals secured before fieldwork; heightened care given the target population's vulnerability.

Encourages diverse, cross-disciplinary teams; Round V earmarks additional funding for teams including researchers with lived experience of displacement and for evaluations of refugee-led organizations.

submission.mechanism: Two-stage: mandatory Expression of Interest, then a full proposal by the round deadline. Off-cycle proposals (≤$75K) accepted with time-sensitive justification.
steps: Choose the grant type matching your project stage (Exploratory / Pilot / Full study / Infrastructure & public goods / Evidence Use / Conference Travel).
Submit the mandatory Expression of Interest (Round V: due May 15, 2026).
Submit the full proposal (Round V: due July 24, 2026).
materials: For full studies: statistical power estimates
submission.notes: Questions and off-cycle inquiries: displacement@poverty-action.org. IPA/J-PAL can help match practitioners with academic researchers.

name: ILAB Grant: Combat Child & Forced Labor in Critical Mineral Supply Chains
funder: U.S. Department of Labor — Bureau of International Labor Affairs (ILAB)
description: Federal funding to combat child labor and forced labor in critical mineral supply chains — directly on ETC's forced-labor / supply-chain traceability work. Surfaced via Tavily discovery from grants.gov.

criteria.label: Mission alignment
criteria.rationale: Child/forced labor in critical mineral supply chains maps almost perfectly onto ETC's forced-labor and supply-chain traceability focus areas and its verifiable-ethical-claims work.

criteria.label: Funding fit
criteria.rationale: ILAB's $9M cooperative agreements typically fund multi-year, field-based program implementation (monitoring, capacity-building in producer countries), not applied research and prototyping; the size and structure poorly match ETC's researcher/staff-time and prototype model.

criteria.label: Competitiveness
criteria.rationale: ILAB awards overwhelmingly go to established international-development implementers (ILO, Verité, Winrock, Solidarity Center) with on-the-ground presence and past DOL performance; ETC would be uncompetitive as a lead but plausible as a tech/traceability subrecipient.

criteria.label: Effort / feasibility
criteria.rationale: Federal cooperative agreements demand heavy proposals—detailed logframes, monitoring/evaluation plans, extensive budgets, past-performance narratives—and onerous reporting, straining ETC's limited grant-writing bandwidth.

criteria.label: Strategic value
criteria.rationale: A federal DOL award would meaningfully elevate ETC's forced-labor/traceability portfolio and open institutional relationships, but the strategic upside is more realistic through a partnering role than a solo lead.

redFlags: Scope mismatch: ILAB funds large-scale international program implementation and field monitoring, not lab-to-field prototyping—likely requires on-the-ground operations in mineral-producing countries outside ETC's wheelhouse.
$9M award size implies extensive field staffing and subgrantee management ETC is not structured to lead.
Eligibility and scoring strongly favor organizations with prior DOL/ILAB past performance and international field presence; ETC has none as lead.
Heavy federal application and compliance/reporting burden relative to ETC's bandwidth.
scoring.summary: The topical fit is excellent—this is squarely ETC's forced-labor and supply-chain traceability terrain—but the grant is a large federal implementation cooperative agreement, not an applied-research/prototyping award, and ILAB overwhelmingly funds experienced international-development implementers with field presence. ETC should not pursue this as a lead; instead explore joining a lead implementer's consortium as the traceability/tech-prototyping partner, where its NYU CGA + Microsoft Research credibility adds distinctive value at manageable effort.
